This mNAV calculator measures how much premium or discount the market puts on a Bitcoin treasury stock like MicroStrategy, MetaPlanet or Semler Scientific versus the raw Bitcoin it owns. It computes BTC NAV as holdings times BTC price, then mNAV = market cap divided by BTC NAV. An mNAV of 1.0× means the stock trades exactly at the value of its coins; above 1.5× is a premium, below 1.0× is a discount. Premium percent is (mNAV − 1) × 100, and premium amount is the dollar gap.

title: Bitcoin vs Strategy (MSTR) Arbitrage Strategy | SimpleFX
snippet:
Strategy (ticker MSTR, formerly known as MicroStrategy) is known for holding a massive Bitcoin treasury on its balance sheet. Since 2020, founder Michael Saylor has raised capital (via equity and debt issuances) to acquire Bitcoin, turning MSTR into a quasi-Bitcoin ETF with leverage.

This means MSTR's stock price closely tracks Bitcoin's price, often with amplified moves. To analyze MSTR's valuation relative to its Bitcoin stash, investors use the Market Cap vs BTC Net Asset Value (NAV) metric, often called mNAV.
...
- Bitcoin NAV: Total market value of Strategy's Bitcoin holdings (BTC held × BTC price)
- mNAV Ratio: MSTR's market capitalization ÷ its Bitcoin NAV
...
- mNAV > 1: MSTR trades at a premium – investors pay above the value of the underlying BTC
- mNAV < 1: MSTR trades at a discount – stock is priced below the value of its Bitcoin holdings

Why does a premium exist? Strategy effectively acts as a leveraged Bitcoin vehicle. Management's strategy of issuing shares/debt to buy more BTC can increase BTC per share over time, giving shareholders exposure to more BTC than the company originally had (a kind of "Bitcoin yield").

Investors often pay a premium for MSTR because they expect outperformance versus holding BTC directly – essentially betting on Saylor's ability to grow the BTC stash and on the company's leveraged upside. For example, a +10% move in BTC has historically led to an ~+15% move in MSTR stock on average (beta > 1), due to this leverage and market premi

title: Microstrategy (MSTR) - NAV Premium Arbitrage - 40% Upside - Special Situation Investments
snippet:
Let me start by saying that I do not have no strong opinion on Bitcoin or MSTR’s software business. MSTR sports $27bn market cap, is very liquid and covered widely by crypto and stock investors from both short and long sides. This is very far from an ‘undiscovered gem’ trade. However, I am keen on one particular aspect – a massive 150% premium to NAV (almost all of it in Bitcoin holdings) that the company is currently trading at. Not only is this premium completely irrational, it’s also at historical peak levels. This happened a number of times before – NAV premiums of 150%+ did not last long and usually reverted back to the 30%-50% levels. Unlike before, this time investors can easily hedge out exposure to Bitcoin (as we now have listed spot ETFs) and bet mainly on the premium reverting to more normalized levels. That’s the core of my short thesis on MSTR – or as Mark Twain said, history doesn’t repeat itself, but it often rhymes.
...
Microstrategy has always traded at a premium to its Bitcoin holdings. Until recently, that sort of made sense as MSTR used to be one of the few available options for investors seeking crypto exposure without the hassle of buying Bitcoin directly (regulation, setting up crypto exchange accounts, managing wallets, dealing with private keys, etc.). There simply weren’t many alternatives. title: MicroStrategies NAV Premium Is Too High
snippet:
the NAV premium
- Chanos trades the NAV by shorting MicroStrategy and buying Bitcoin
...
The main problem Chanos currently sees for MicroStrategy is the company's premium to its NAV. Generally speaking, an investment company almost always trades below its NAV. The reason for this is that when investing in a company that only holds assets, you always run the risk of the manager doing something unexpected or fraudulent. Nevertheless, MSTR trades at a huge premium of 2.7 to its underlying assets (Bitcoins), raising the question of why this is the case.
...
According to Chanos, the premium does not make any sense for the following two reasons. Firstly, Microstrategy does not provide any additional value other than selling convertible debt and buying Bitcoin that would justify a premium to Bitcoin because of future growth. Secondly, there is nothing proprietary about Microstrategies' strategy. Every other company can replicate it, which should reduce the premium in the long term due to more and more competition in the space. Another big question that is raised by Chanos is whether the premium on NAV could even be necessary for MicroStrategies' business model. What he touches on here is that new buyers of MSTR basically buy Bitcoin for a far higher price than it's currently traded for, which increases the BTC/share ratio for previous buyers. This means that you only get a lower market price for BTC by buying MSTR shares, if enough investors buy it later on to push down your own BTC
